newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Leading Russian shares ease as lesser known rally.
newsitem.headline: Leading Russian shares ease as lesser known rally.

text.p: Investors on Monday dropped Russian leading shares to pick up less well known stocks in a trend which traders said would continue over the short term but which would be overtaken eventually by a new wave of investment in major shares.

"Second-tier telecoms, preferreds, and the preferreds of second-tier telecoms are all increasing in interest. There has been some spectacular movement and I think it is continuing," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell researcher Jim Nail.
The Russian Trading System 24-share index firmed 1.26 percent to 190.65 on $13.8 million turnover for the market, relatively low volume compared to recent activity.
Toward the end of open trading Saint Petersburg International Telephone (MMT) had risen sharply. Ordinaries rose to $21.40 from $17.00 at Friday's close. Prefs rose to $13.30 from $11.28.
Leading share UES, one of the most heavily traded for months, ticked down to $0.0835 from $0.0839 while its preferred shares rose to $0.0670 from $0.0641.
"There is only modest demand for blue chips. The only ones buying them are the ones who have traditionally bought them," said UCB head trader Dmitry Yevenko.
Analysts saw short term pressure on leading shares tomorrow, and carrying through until the end of the year.
"Tomorrow the market should be stronger on average, but I do not want to answer for all the paper," said Rinako Plus trader Alexander Lobanov.
Troika-Dialog's Robert Devane said old investors were looking for new gold.
"The activity in the market now is being driven by the investors who were here early on -- private investors, hedge funds, and the like," he said.
"These $10-20 million hedge funds would rather be in the lesser known stocks, but they need to sell blue chips to get there."

Larger, newer investors were seen entering the market and heading for the traditionally sought, more liquid stocks, but analysts said there could be a time lag, especially before the beginning of the year, before much new money trickled in.
"There are prospects of about 20 percent per year equity price gains in most of the blue chips," Nail said.
